options: An AC ground: equal and opposite currents leave it unchanged
questions.explanation: For purely differential drive, one device's current rises as much as the other's falls, so nothing flows in the tail resistance.

questions.prompt: In the common-mode half circuit, what does the tail resistance \(R_{SS}\) become?
options: \(2R_{SS}\) in the source of each half
questions.explanation: Both halves push current into the same \(R_{SS}\), so the voltage across it is \(2iR_{SS}\); splitting it gives each half \(2R_{SS}\).

questions.explanation: The DM half is a CS stage with a grounded source, so \(v_{od}/v_{DM} = g_mR_D = 12\) (Eq. 16.41); the tail resistance plays no part.

questions.prompt: A pair has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_D = 5\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) per side and \(R_{SS} = 20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find the common-mode gain to one output.
questions.explanation: The CM half is a degenerated CS stage with \(2R_{SS}\): \(A_{CM} = -g_mR_D/(1 + 2g_mR_{SS}) = -10/81 = -0.123\) (Eq. 16.45).

questions.prompt: Why can't the half-circuit method be applied blindly to a pair whose two loads differ?
options: Asymmetry couples common-mode input into differential output, so the two modes no longer separate
Because the tail current changes sign
It can; symmetry is never needed
questions.explanation: The method rests on mirror symmetry; for a symmetric circuit the CM-to-DM gain is zero (Eq. 16.46).
